title: Uber Ordered to Pay $40 Million After Driver Abandons UCLA Grad on California Freeway
snippet: A California arbitrator has ordered Uber to pay $40 million to the grieving parents of a 23-year-old UCLA graduate who was hit and killed after her driver kicked her out on a freeway.
content:
A California arbitrator has ordered Uber to pay $40 million to the family of a UCLA graduate who was tragically struck and killed after her driver forced her and a friend out of the vehicle along a busy Southern California freeway.

Emily Normandin-Parker, 23, died in the early morning hours of August 12, 2023. She and her friend, Luna Moore, had hailed an Uber following a night out in Costa Mesa. When Moore became sick and vomited inside the vehicle, driver Vu Tran pulled over on State Route 73 at a dangerous "gore point"—the neutral area separating an exit ramp from freeway traffic—and demanded both passengers exit the vehicle.

'More Worry for His New Car Than His Passengers'

While Tran argued with Moore on the side of the highway over a vehicle cleaning fee, Normandin-Parker was struck by oncoming traffic. Following a five-day arbitration hearing, retired Los Angeles County Judge Richard A. Stone awarded $20 million each to Normandin-Parker's parents, Carol Normandin and Ken Parker. Moore was awarded $300,000.

In a scathing ruling, Judge Stone scolded Tran for demonstrating "far more worry for his new car than he did for his passengers," finding that the driver needlessly created a life-threatening situation by stopping illegally on the highway. Attorneys representing the family also noted that Tran had a history of passenger complaints regarding unsafe driving, with prior riders describing him as reckless.

Family Rejects Non-Disclosure Demands

Normandin-Parker's parents revealed that shortly after the ruling, Uber attempted to enforce strict confidentiality, sending an agreement with a $10 million penalty clause if the family spoke out publicly. The parents chose to speak out to raise awareness about rideshare safety and prevent future tragedies.

"Emily did everything Uber tells riders to do—she made the responsible choice not to drive and we trusted Uber to get her home safely," her parents said. "That trust cost our daughter her life."

Uber issued a statement offering sympathy to the family but pushed back against the ruling, claiming the arbitrator was wrong to hold the company legally responsible for the incident. The company noted that it has updated driver guidelines regarding unsafe drop-off points.

To honor the memory of the Laguna Beach native, who graduated from UCLA's School of Theater, Film and Television, her family created the Emily Normandin-Parker Foundation to campaign for stricter safety standards across the rideshare industry.
